summary:
Article 319 of Senegal's 1965 Penal Code criminalises an "improper or unnatural act" with a person of the same sex, carrying one to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 1,500,000 CFA francs. The maximum penalty is always applied where the act involves a person under 21. The provision is drafted around the sex of the participants and makes no reference to transgender status, gender identity or gender expression.

An amendment adopted on 12 March 2026, signed 30 March and published 31 March raises the penalty to five to ten years' imprisonment and fines of 100,000 to 10,000,000 CFA francs. The bill, presented 25 February 2026, adds an explicit ban on the promotion, financing and support of homosexuality, bisexuality and transsexuality, together with a penalty for abusive relationships conducted in bad faith, and targets organisations promoting LGBT content through film, television or writing.

Senegal provides no legal gender recognition procedure. In the 2009 and 2013 Universal Periodic Reviews, Senegal rejected recommendations to decriminalise same-sex conduct and to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, maintaining criminal liability and enforcement risk. Recommendations to establish a moratorium on Article 319 and to criminalise orientation-based violence were likewise refused, on the stated ground that being homosexual is not a crime though same-sex acts are. There are no laws broadly protecting LGBTQ people against discrimination; only limited prohibitions on revealing or stigmatising depiction of sexual orientation exist.

Enforcement is documented and ongoing. In December 2008, nine men were arrested in a Dakar flat and in January 2009 convicted to five years for indecent conduct and unnatural acts plus three years for membership of a criminal group, amid repeated torture in police custody; convictions were overturned in April 2009 with immediate release. In September 2018, two men and two women were arrested in Dakar after videos circulated in their neighbourhood. In early February 2026, 22 gay men were arrested within two weeks, including a 20 February detention at the Senegal-Gambian border while attempting to leave the country. In August, 99 men were arrested, 28 released and 71 facing up to 20 years after the doubling of the maximum. Police have arrested individuals on second-hand reports alone; two women detained in January after a kissing video circulated were released on bail without formal charge, and in October four men received four-year sentences plus a 200,000 CFA franc fine for acts against nature alongside arms and battery convictions, with a third man receiving three years.

Physical violence against LGBT people is documented. In November 2023, the body of Cheikh Fall, a 31-year-old man outed as gay, was exhumed and burned in the street in Kaolack on 28 October 2023, with four suspected masterminds apprehended 30 October 2023 and images showing a crowd of hundreds around the fire. Around mid-2009, bodies of deceased goor-gigen (man-woman) were dug up from cemeteries, including a May 2009 Thies case where a corpse reputed homosexual was twice disinterred. In December 2012, a gay male couple was beaten near Dakar by a parent. Transgender persons within the LGBT category are described as often facing criminal prosecution, arrest, discrimination, intolerance and violence; local groups maintain an exceedingly low profile and media rarely report hatred or violence. On 6 February 2009, it was recorded that the president had authorised a homosexual to change his name to a woman's name, indicating past allowance of name change reflecting feminine presentation.

Political figures have faced prosecution for speech touching on the issue: a political activist and a preacher were jailed and fined 100,000 CFA francs each after posting a video attacking opposition leader Ousmane Sonko for allowing a visiting French politician to express support for same-sex marriage. The US State Department's 2012 Human Rights Report listed violence and discrimination against LGBT persons among Senegal's major human-rights problems. Anti-LGBT forces have pushed since 2020 for 15-year sentences, up from the then maximum of five years.
tangentialFactors:
Advocacy for harsher penalties predates the 2026 amendment: anti-LGBT forces had pushed since 2020 for 15-year sentences, up from the then maximum of five years, and the government's February 2026 draft went further still in fine levels. Arrests have clustered around political moments, including the run-up to the 2019 elections and the circulation of videos, suggesting that enforcement intensity can rise with political competition rather than with any change in the law.

The 2026 amendment's ban on promotion, financing and support of homosexuality, bisexuality and transsexuality, and its targeting of organisations promoting LGBT content through film, television or writing, extends exposure beyond conduct to advocacy, media and civil-society activity. Local LGBT groups already maintain an exceedingly low profile because of stigma and the legal regime, and media rarely report hatred or violence, so documentation of incidents should be treated as a floor rather than a measure of prevalence.

There are no laws broadly protecting LGBTQ people against discrimination, with only limited prohibitions on revealing or stigmatising depiction of sexual orientation. In the 2009 and 2013 Universal Periodic Reviews, Senegal rejected recommendations to decriminalise same-sex conduct, to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, to establish a moratorium on Article 319, and to criminalise orientation-based violence, maintaining criminal liability and enforcement risk for residents. Local LGBT groups maintain an exceedingly low profile due to the laws and stigma, and media rarely report hatred or violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not establish whether the 2026 amendment's ban on promotion, financing and support has been used in any prosecution to date, or how courts will interpret "abusive relationships conducted in bad faith." The August arrests of 99 men, with 71 facing up to 20 years, are reported without a specific year in the source and their date is unresolved here.

No current survey data on transgender people's own experiences of violence, healthcare or document screening in Senegal appears in the inventory; the violence figures available are individual documented incidents. Whether any entry, visa or border screening process flags gender markers or gender presentation is not sourced. The US State Department human-rights report cited is from 2012 and is historical.
